raw_case_text:
In late July, a 36-year-old African American man with a history of HIV and remote history of properly treated syphilis, presented to our institution for a second opinion regarding his recent diagnosis of peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (PTCL-NOS). The patient's history revealed he had not been on anti-retroviral therapy (ART) for many years due to adverse effects. During the evaluation by his outside practitioner, he was told that his viral load was "very high", but uncertain in the number, though his CD4 count was 325 cells/ml. He was thus started on a combination of elvitegravir, cobicistat, tenofovir, and emtricitabine. Two weeks after restarting ART, he reported fevers, chills, night sweats and several erupting skin lesions on his jaw, scalp, nose, legs, and arms. Follow-up CD4 count revealed a moderate increase up to 450 cells/ml.
In June, during his initial work-up at an outside facility, a skin biopsy was done on a right scalp lesion and revealed an atypical lymphohistiocytic infiltrate in the subcutaneous tissue, consisting mainly of CD3+, CD5+, CD7+, and CD8+ cells. Histiocytes were positive for CD68 marker, and the T-cell receptor (TCR) gene was clonally rearranged. Successively, a computed tomography (CT) scan of his neck, chest, and abdomen demonstrated several prominent lymph nodes in the neck, axillary, and inguinal areas, ranging from 14 mm up to 19 mm. A biopsy of the terminal ileum and of a rectal mass, which revealed on the former CT scan, were performed. The pathology of the terminal ileum showed an atypical submucosal lymphoid infiltrate consisting of 50% CD8+ and 50% CD4+ cells. The biopsy of the rectal mass showed atypical lymphoid cells in a necrotic background. The bone marrow biopsy was performed and showed normocellular marrow (40-60% cellularity) with regular trilinear hematopoiesis. No abnormal lymphoid population was detected using flow cytometry, and cytogenetics was normal 46, XY. Further inguinal and peripheral lymph node biopsies failed to show evidence of lymphoma. The differential at this time consisted of PTCL NOS versus CD8+ aggressive epidermotropic cytotoxic T-cell lymphoma. The patient underwent port placement and was to begin chemotherapy. It was at this time that he presented to us.
On initial presentation, the patient exhibited on his nose, forehead, scalp, cheek, neck, and bilateral upper and lower extremities, several large one to two inch, discrete, yellowish-brown, necrotic crusted malodorous verrucous plaques and tumors (Figures 1 and 2). He reported that the large plaque on his nose was occluding his nares and draining a foul-smelling brownish fluid, making it difficult for him to breath. At this time, he was not experiencing fever, chills, or night sweats, but did continue to endorse some unintentional weight loss. The lesion located on his right arm was quite painful, making it difficult to sleep, but there were no intraoral lesions present. At this time, further skin biopsies were performed. The pathology (Figures 3A and B) showed an atypical lymphohistiocytic infiltrate that appeared to be reactive without clonal etiology. There were areas of necrosis and no discrete granulomas. The epidermis showed spongiosis, keratinocyte necrosis; acute inflammatory infiltrate, and pseudo-epitheliomatous hyperplasia with flow cytometry of the skin specimen showed predominantly small mature lymphocytes and histiocytes with no clonal findings and no evidence of T-cell lymphoma. Acid-fast bacilli (AFB), cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex and varicella zoster viruses, and Warthin-Starry staining were negative. AFB, fungal, and bacterial cultures were also negative. Throughout this work-up, the patient reported that his lesions were only getting worse, and his nasal breathing problems were also increasing.
After effectively ruling out cutanous lymphoma, secondary syphilis of the rupioid type became top of our differential. The fluorescent treponemal antibody (FTA-ABS) was positive, and the rapid plasma reagin titer was very highly reactive at 1:1,024. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies were negative. In conjunction with the time course and increase in his CD4 count after starting ART, it was thought that his rupioid syphilis was derived from an immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). He was consequently commenced on intravenous penicillin G (IV) 24 million units daily but after about 24 hours from initiation, he developed fever and chills. It was unclear if this was due to an allergic reaction or secondary to a mild Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, which is expected during treatment for rupioid syphilis. However, the dose was decreased and within days, the lesions began resolving and the patients breathing improved. He was treated in this manner for two weeks and then discharged with an additional three weekly injections of intramuscular benzathine penicillin 2.4 million units. The crusted lesions flaked off within a week of treatment. Within several weeks of treatment, all of the cutaneous lesions were resolved, but the patient was subsequently lost to follow-up without reevaluation of his intra-abdominal lesions.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 36-year-old African American HIV-positive man presented in late July for a second opinion regarding a recent outside diagnosis of peripheral T-cell lymphoma after developing eruptive, malodorous, necrotic verrucous plaques over his face, scalp, and extremities 2 weeks after restarting antiretroviral therapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Off ART for many years due to side effects, the patient had restarted elvitegravir/cobicistat/tenofovir/emtricitabine in June at an outside clinic (at baseline CD4 count 325 cells/mL and 'very high' HIV viral load). Two weeks after starting ART, he developed fevers, chills, night sweats, and eruptive skin tumors across his scalp, nose, jaw, arms, and legs, along with cervical/axillary/inguinal lymphadenopathy and terminal ileal and rectal masses on CT. Outside scalp, ileal, and rectal biopsies showed an atypical CD8+/CD3+/CD5+/CD7+ lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with clonal TCR rearrangement, leading to a misdiagnosis of peripheral T-cell lymphoma (PTCL-NOS) and port placement for chemotherapy before he sought a second opinion with worsening nasal airway obstruction and right arm pain.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of HIV infection (previously off ART for years; restarted elvitegravir/cobicistat/tenofovir/emtricitabine ~6 weeks prior); remote history of treated syphilis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for unintentional weight loss, foul-smelling nasal obstruction impairing breathing, and severe right arm lesion pain impairing sleep; initial fever, chills, and night sweats had subsided by presentation. Home medication: elvitegravir/cobicistat/tenofovir/emtricitabine.

objective.physical_examination: Cutaneous examination revealed multiple discrete, 1-to-2-inch, yellowish-brown, necrotic, crusted, malodorous verrucous plaques and tumors involving the nose (occluding the nares and draining foul brownish fluid), forehead, scalp, cheek, neck, and bilateral upper and lower extremities; no intraoral lesions were present.
objective.routine_investigations: Syphilis serologies were strongly positive with a fluorescent treponemal antibody-absorption (FTA-ABS) test and a rapid plasma reagin (RPR) titer of 1:1,024. Skin biopsy AFB, fungal, and bacterial cultures were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-cell count had risen from 325 cells/mL pre-ART to 450 cells/mL. Prior neck/chest/abdominal CT showed 14–19 mm cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymphadenopathy and terminal ileal/rectal masses; bone marrow biopsy (normocellular 40–60%, 46,XY) and inguinal/peripheral node biopsies were negative for lymphoma. Repeat skin biopsy histopathology and flow cytometry at our institution demonstrated epidermal spongiosis, keratinocyte necrosis, pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, and a polyclonal reactive lymphohistiocytic infiltrate without T-cell lymphoma clonality (negative AFB, CMV, HSV, VZV, and Warthin-Starry stains). Lumbar puncture CSF analysis was negative for neurosyphilis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Rupioid secondary/malignant syphilis presenting as unmasking immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) 2 weeks after initiating elvitegravir/cobicistat/tenofovir/emtricitabine in a 36-year-old HIV-positive man (CD4+ count rising from 325 to 450 cells/mL), initially misdiagnosed at an outside hospital as peripheral T-cell lymphoma (PTCL-NOS) due to pseudolymphomatous cutaneous/gastrointestinal infiltrates with pseudoclonal TCR rearrangement. Confirmed by RPR titer 1:1,024, positive FTA-ABS, polyclonal flow cytometry on repeat skin biopsy, and rapid complete clinical resolution on penicillin therapy. Treated with intravenous aqueous penicillin G (initiated at 24 million units/day, dose-adjusted after a mild 24-hour Jarisch-Herxheimer febrile reaction, and continued for 2 weeks) followed by three weekly intramuscular injections of benzathine penicillin G (2.4 million units), achieving sloughing of crusts within 1 week and complete resolution of all cutaneous lesions within several weeks.
